topic.title: Algebraic fractions with numerical denominators: simplifying and solving equations
topic.subject: maths
topic.examWeightHint: Two items most series. An 'add these two algebraic fractions' of 2-3 marks mid-paper (Summer 2025 M3 Q12, where only a third succeeded and over half could not start), and a fractional equation of 3-4 marks late on (Summer 2023 M3 Q19 at about 10% full marks, November 2025 M3 Q29, Summer 2026 M3 Q27). M4 re-uses the same skill as an opener (Summer 2025 Q3, November 2024 Q9).
mustMemorise: Lowest common denominator of the numbers, then multiply each numerator by what its denominator was multiplied by
A subtracted numerator stays in brackets; when the bracket goes, every sign inside it changes
To solve, multiply EVERY term on BOTH sides by the LCD — constants included
Never convert to decimals: one third is not 0.33
Substitute the answer back into the original equation as a check
notOnThisSpec: Denominators containing the unknown, such as 2/(x + 1) — those are M4-NA-03 and M4-NA-04
Any equation that clears to a quadratic: at M3 the equation stays linear
Simplifying a fraction by factorising and cancelling is statement M3-NA-09, the next topic

note.title: Algebraic fractions with numerical denominators
note.subject: maths

mustKnow: a/p ± b/q = (aq ± bp)/pq, with the LCD used where it is smaller
Minus a bracket changes every sign inside it
To clear denominators, multiply every term on both sides by the LCD

notOnThisSpec: Denominators containing the unknown, such as 2/(x + 1) — those are M4-NA-03 and M4-NA-04
Any equation that clears to a quadratic: at M3 the equation stays linear
Simplifying a fraction by factorising and cancelling is statement M3-NA-09, the next topic

mustBeAbleTo: Find the lowest common denominator of two numerical denominators and rewrite both fractions over it
Add or subtract two algebraic fractions and give a single fraction in its simplest form
Keep a subtracted numerator in brackets and change every sign when the bracket is removed
Handle a multiplier outside a fraction, such as 2(x + 1)/3
Solve an equation by multiplying every term on both sides by the lowest common denominator
Solve an equation with the unknown on both sides and a fraction on each side
Set up such an equation from words or from a context, and say what the answer means
Keep every line exact rather than converting to decimals
Check a solution by substituting it back into the original equation
sheet.howExamined: M3 (calculator, 2 hours, 100 marks), and again with no calculator in M7 Paper 1. Two items are usual: an addition or subtraction of two algebraic fractions worth 2-3 marks in the middle of the paper, and a fractional equation worth 3-4 marks near the end. Schemes give M1 for the common denominator or for multiplying every term by the LCD, A1 for the correctly bracketed numerators or the cleared line, then MA1 per expansion or collection line and a final accuracy mark for the value of the unknown.
traps: Not knowing where to start: over half the candidates in Summer 2025 M3 Q12 could not begin the addition
Adding numerators and denominators separately, so 2/3 + 1/4 becomes 3/7
Multiplying only part of a side — the 4 multiplied but the −2x beside it left alone (November 2024 M3 Q23)
Multiplying the numerator by the denominator as well as cancelling it, an incorrect first line with no follow-through (Summer 2025 M4 Q3)
Subtracting only the first term of a bracketed numerator (Summer 2025 M4 Q21)
Converting to decimals and rounding, which cost one or two marks in Summer 2023 M3 Q19 and again in Summer 2023 M4 Q8
Expanding a bracket after clearing the fraction and losing a sign (November 2025 M4 Q14)

Slipping on the last line once the fraction has been cleared, by dividing the wrong way round or by dropping the minus sign; the method marks survive that, the final mark does not (November 2024 M4 Q9)

steps.working: Lowest common denominator of 4 and 6 is 12.
steps.decision: The LCM of the denominators, not their product. $4 \times 6 = 24$ works too, but 12 keeps the numbers small and means no cancelling at the end.

options: 12 is the smallest number both 4 and 6 divide into
12 is always the common denominator for two fractions

steps.decision: $12 \div 4 = 3$, so the first numerator is multiplied by 3; $12 \div 6 = 2$, so the second is multiplied by 2. Each numerator stays inside a bracket until it is expanded.
One denominator now, so the numerators simply add. Expand each bracket on this line and nothing else.
Collect like terms. Check whether anything cancels: 13 and 7 share no factor with 12, so this is simplest form.
3 and 5 share no factor, so the LCD is their product. The second numerator is being subtracted, so it stays inside its bracket.
Expand each product, but keep the subtracted one bracketed for one more line. This is the line where the marks are usually lost.

options: Because the whole of $3(x + 4)$ is subtracted, not just the $3x$
Because a numerator must always be written in brackets
whyMenu.explain: The minus sign applies to the entire second numerator, and the bracket keeps that visible until it is removed.

steps.decision: Remove the bracket by changing **every** sign inside it: $+3x$ becomes $-3x$ and $+12$ becomes $-12$.
Collect. The numerator has a common factor 22, so $\dfrac{22(x - 1)}{15}$ is equally acceptable; 22 and 15 share no factor, so the fraction will not reduce further.

steps.decision: The LCM of 2 and 3 is 6, and 6 would clear both fractions; 12 is used here to match the diagram, and any common multiple works. **Every** term is multiplied, including the 5 on the right.

options: Because an equation stays balanced only if both sides are multiplied by the same amount
Because the fractions are on the left, so only the left side changes
Because the 5 has no denominator, so it is left alone
whyMenu.explain: Multiplying one side alone breaks the equation. The 5 is $\frac{5}{1}$, and it becomes 60.

steps.decision: $12 \div 2 = 6$ and $12 \div 3 = 4$. The denominators are gone; what is left is an ordinary linear equation with brackets.
Expand each bracket term by term, then collect. Keeping the expansion on its own line makes any slip easy to find.
Solve as usual. Then substitute back: $\dfrac{8}{2} + \dfrac{3}{3} = 4 + 1 = 5$. The check costs ten seconds and confirms the sign work.

workedExamples.stem:
A water butt holds $x$ litres when full.

On Monday a quarter of the water is used. On Tuesday a sixth of the original amount is used. Altogether 75 litres are used.

Form an equation in $x$ and solve it.

steps.decision: 'A quarter of $x$' is $\frac{x}{4}$ and 'a sixth of $x$' is $\frac{x}{6}$. Writing the equation is a mark in itself, so it goes on the page before any solving.
LCM of 4 and 6 is 12. $12 \div 4 = 3$ and $12 \div 6 = 2$, and the 75 becomes $12 \times 75 = 900$.

options: $12 \times 75 = 900$, because the right-hand side is multiplied as well
The 75 stays as it is, because it has no denominator
The 75 is divided by 12 to balance the left side
whyMenu.explain: Every term on both sides is multiplied by the same number, which is what keeps the equation true.

steps.decision: Collect and divide. The answer is a number of litres, so it should look sensible for a water butt.
Substituting back into the original words, not just the equation, catches a setup error as well as an arithmetic one.

twin.stem: Deirdre thinks of a number $n$. She adds 5 and halves the result. She also subtracts 1 from $n$ and divides by 3. The two answers add to 8. Form an equation in $n$ and solve it.

items.stem: What is the lowest common denominator for $\dfrac{2x}{3} + \dfrac{x}{4}$?

options.feedback: The smallest number both 3 and 4 divide into. Their product, 12, happens to be the LCM here because they share no factor.
The denominators were added. A common denominator has to be a multiple of both, and 7 is a multiple of neither.
4 does not divide into 3, so the second fraction cannot be rewritten over 3.

items.skill: Rewrite a fraction over a larger denominator

options.feedback: The denominator was multiplied by 3, so the numerator is too — and the whole numerator, kept in a bracket.
Only the denominator changed, which changes the value of the fraction. Whatever is done below the line must be done above it.
Only the $x$ was multiplied by 3. The 3 in the numerator is part of the same expression and must be multiplied too, giving $3x + 9$.
$5x - (x + 2) = 5x - x - 2 = 4x - 2$. The minus sign reaches both terms of the second numerator.
Only the $x$ was subtracted. Removing the bracket changes the sign of every term inside it, so $+2$ becomes $-2$.
The numerators were added. The operation between the fractions is a subtraction.

items.stem: To solve $\dfrac{x}{5} + 2 = 7$, you multiply every term by 5. What does the 2 become?
items.skill: Multiply every term, including the constants

options.feedback: Every term on both sides is multiplied by 5, so 2 becomes 10 and 7 becomes 35, giving $x + 10 = 35$.
Leaving the 2 alone unbalances the equation. November 2024 M3 Q23 reported exactly this: one term on a side multiplied and the other not.
That divides instead of multiplying. The aim is to clear the denominator, so every term is multiplied by 5.

items.stem: Solving $\dfrac{2x + 1}{3} = 5$, what is the correct first line?

options.feedback: Multiplying both sides by 3 cancels the denominator on the left and turns the 5 into 15.
The numerator was multiplied by 3 as well as the denominator cancelled, so the left side has been multiplied twice. Summer 2025 M4 Q3 reported this as an incorrect first line with no follow-through.
The right side was divided instead of multiplied. To undo a division by 3, multiply.

items.stem: Solving $\dfrac{x}{2} + \dfrac{x}{3} = 1$, a student writes $0.5x + 0.33x = 1$. What is the risk?

options.text: 0.33 is not exactly one third, so the answer will be slightly out
options.feedback: $\frac{1}{3} = 0.333...$; rounding it loses accuracy marks. Clearing the denominators keeps everything exact.

options.text: There is no risk, decimals are always fine
options.feedback: Summer 2023 M3 Q19 reported candidates who converted to decimals losing one or two marks through rounding.

options.text: Decimals cannot be used in algebra
options.feedback: They can, but a recurring decimal has to be rounded, and that is where the accuracy goes. Multiplying by 6 avoids the problem entirely.

items.stem: In $\dfrac{3(x - 2)}{4} = 6$, what is the first line after multiplying by 4?
items.skill: Clear a denominator with a bracket above it

options.feedback: The 4 cancels on the left and the 6 becomes 24. The bracket is expanded on the next line, not this one.
The bracket was removed without multiplying the $-2$ by 3. November 2025 M4 Q14 reported expansions of this shape going wrong.
The right side was not multiplied. Both sides get the same treatment.

items.stem: You solved a fractional equation and got $x = 4$. What is the quickest way to be sure?

options.text: Put 4 back into the original equation and see whether both sides agree
options.feedback: Ten seconds, and it catches sign slips and expansion errors alike. It is the best habit on this topic.

options.text: Check the answer is a whole number
options.feedback: Fractional equations often have fractional answers; being a whole number proves nothing.
Re-reading tends to repeat the same thinking. Substituting tests the answer independently.

hints: The denominators already match, so only the numerators are combined.

commonErrors.feedback: Only the $x$ was subtracted. When the bracket comes off, every sign inside it changes, so $+2$ becomes $-2$.

hints: 10 is already a multiple of 5, so 10 is the lowest common denominator.

commonErrors.feedback: Numerators and denominators were added separately. Rewrite both fractions over 10 first, then add only the numerators.

hints: Removing the subtracted bracket turns $-6$ into $+6$.

commonErrors.feedback: The $-6$ kept its sign. Minus a bracket changes every term inside it, so $-6$ becomes $+6$ and the numerator is $x + 10$.

parts.stem: Write $\dfrac{3x + 1}{4} + \dfrac{2x - 5}{6}$ as one fraction, fully simplified.
hints: The LCM of 4 and 6 is 12, not 24.

commonErrors.feedback: Only the $x$ terms were multiplied up. The multiplier applies to the whole numerator, so $3(3x + 1) = 9x + 3$.
Numerators and denominators were combined separately. Over half the candidates in Summer 2025 M3 Q12 did not know where to begin; the first move is always the common denominator.

hints: 5 and 2 share no factor, so the LCD is 10.

commonErrors.feedback: $5(x - 3)$ came out as $5x + 15$. Multiplying a bracket keeps the sign of each term, so it is $5x - 15$.

context.setting: Pure algebra, subtraction with a multi-term numerator

hints: Keep the subtracted numerator in a bracket until it is expanded.

commonErrors.feedback: The $+12$ kept its sign after the bracket was removed. Both terms change: $-3x - 12$. The Summer 2025 report noted that only a small number reached full marks once more than one term had to be subtracted.
The $+1$ was not turned into $-1$. Removing a subtracted bracket changes every sign inside it.

context.setting: Pure algebra, a multiplier outside a fraction

hints: The 2 outside is part of the first numerator: it is $\dfrac{2x + 2}{3}$.
LCD 12, so the first numerator is multiplied by 4 and the second by 3.

commonErrors.feedback: The 2 outside the first bracket was dropped, giving $4(x + 1)$ instead of $8(x + 1)$. Turn $\dfrac{2(x+1)}{3}$ into $\dfrac{2x+2}{3}$ first and the multiplier cannot be missed.

hints: 7 and 2 share no factor, so the LCD is 14.

commonErrors.feedback: The constants were not multiplied up: $7(x + 5)$ is $7x + 35$, not $7x + 5$. Every term of a numerator is multiplied.

context.setting: Pure algebra, one fraction, non-calculator friendly

hints: Multiplying both sides by 4 cancels the denominator on the left.

commonErrors.feedback: The right side was left as 7, giving $5x - 2 = 7$. Multiplying by 4 applies to both sides, so the 7 becomes 28.

parts.workedSolution:
Multiply every term by 6: $3(x + 4) + 2(x - 1) = 30$.
Expand: $3x + 12 + 2x - 2 = 30$.
Collect: $5x + 10 = 30$, so $5x = 20$ and $x = 4$.
Check: $\dfrac{8}{2} + \dfrac{3}{3} = 4 + 1 = 5$.

commonErrors.feedback: The 5 was not multiplied by 6, so the equation became $5x + 10 = 5$. Every term on both sides gets the same multiplier.
Converting to decimals introduced a rounding error. Summer 2023 M3 Q19 reported that decimal routes lost one or two marks; multiplying through by 6 keeps everything exact.

context.setting: Pure algebra, a subtraction of two fractions

scheme.for: 9x − 3 − 2x + 10 = 84, with both signs of the second bracket changed

hints: LCM of 4 and 6 is 12; the 7 becomes 84.
parts.workedSolution:
Multiply every term by 12: $3(3x - 1) - 2(x - 5) = 84$.
Expand: $9x - 3 - 2x + 10 = 84$.
Collect: $7x + 7 = 84$, so $7x = 77$ and $x = 11$.
Check: $\dfrac{32}{4} - \dfrac{6}{6} = 8 - 1 = 7$.

commonErrors.feedback: $-2(x - 5)$ was taken as $-2x - 10$, so the constant came out wrong. The minus multiplies both terms, turning $-5$ into $+10$.

context.setting: Pure algebra, unknown on both sides with two fractions

scheme.for: cross-multiplying or multiplying both sides by 6: 3(x + 9) = 2(2x + 3)

hints: Multiplying both sides by 6 clears both denominators at once.
Gather the $x$ terms on the side that keeps them positive.
parts.workedSolution:
Multiply both sides by 6: $3(x + 9) = 2(2x + 3)$.
Expand: $3x + 27 = 4x + 6$.
Subtract $3x$ and 6 from both sides: $21 = x$.
Check: $\dfrac{30}{2} = 15$ and $\dfrac{45}{3} = 15$.

commonErrors.feedback: Both denominators were simply crossed out, leaving $x + 9 = 2x + 3$ and $x = 6$. Removing a denominator means multiplying **both** sides by it, so the left needs $\times 3$ and the right $\times 2$, giving $3(x + 9) = 2(2x + 3)$. November 2024 M3 Q23 named this: whatever one term is multiplied by, every term on both sides gets the same.

context.setting: Pure algebra, a bracket above a fraction line

scheme.for: 4x + 12 − 5x + 20 = 10, with both signs of the second bracket changed

hints: LCD 10; the 1 on the right becomes 10.
$10 \div 5 = 2$, and that 2 multiplies the whole numerator $2(x + 3)$, giving $4(x + 3)$.
The $x$ coefficient comes out negative; divide by $-1$ at the end.
parts.workedSolution:
Multiply every term by 10: $4(x + 3) - 5(x - 4) = 10$.
Expand: $4x + 12 - 5x + 20 = 10$.
Collect: $-x + 32 = 10$, so $-x = -22$ and $x = 22$.
Check: $\dfrac{2 \times 25}{5} - \dfrac{18}{2} = 10 - 9 = 1$.

commonErrors.feedback: $-5(x - 4)$ came out as $-5x - 20$, so the constant was wrong. November 2025 M4 Q14 reported expansions of this shape going wrong, though follow-through marks were still available.
The 1 on the right was left unmultiplied. Every term on both sides is multiplied by 10, so the right becomes 10.

context.setting: Pure algebra, a fraction on the right-hand side

hints: 6 is a multiple of 6, 3 and 2, so it clears all three fractions.
parts.workedSolution:
Multiply every term by 6: $(2x + 5) + 2(3x - 1) = 27$.
Expand: $2x + 5 + 6x - 2 = 27$.
Collect: $8x + 3 = 27$, so $8x = 24$ and $x = 3$.
Check: $\dfrac{11}{6} + \dfrac{8}{3} = \dfrac{11}{6} + \dfrac{16}{6} = \dfrac{27}{6} = \dfrac{9}{2}$.

commonErrors.feedback: The fractions were turned into decimals and rounded. Keeping them exact, by multiplying every term by 6, avoids the loss entirely.

context.setting: A water butt emptied over two days

parts.stem:
A water butt holds $x$ litres when full.

On Monday a quarter of the full amount is used. On Tuesday a sixth of the full amount is used. Altogether 75 litres are used.

**Form an equation** in $x$ and solve it to find how many litres the butt holds when full.
hints: LCM of 4 and 6 is 12, and the 75 becomes 900.
parts.workedSolution:
$\dfrac{x}{4} + \dfrac{x}{6} = 75$.
Multiply every term by 12: $3x + 2x = 900$, so $5x = 900$ and $x = 180$ litres.
Check: $\dfrac{180}{4} = 45$ and $\dfrac{180}{6} = 30$, and $45 + 30 = 75$.

commonErrors.feedback: The 75 was not multiplied by 12, so the equation became $5x = 75$. Both sides get the same multiplier.
The two fractions were treated as $\dfrac{x}{4} + \dfrac{x}{6} = \dfrac{2x}{10}$. Denominators are never added; rewrite both over 12 or clear them.

context.setting: A number puzzle with two fractional operations

parts.stem:
Deirdre thinks of a number $n$.

She adds 5 to it and halves the result. She also subtracts 1 from $n$ and divides that result by 3.

Her two answers add to 8. Form an equation in $n$ and solve it.
hints: 'Adds 5 then halves' is $\dfrac{n + 5}{2}$, with the whole of $n + 5$ over the 2.
LCM of 2 and 3 is 6; the 8 becomes 48.
parts.workedSolution:
$\dfrac{n + 5}{2} + \dfrac{n - 1}{3} = 8$.
Multiply every term by 6: $3(n + 5) + 2(n - 1) = 48$.
Expand and collect: $3n + 15 + 2n - 2 = 48$, so $5n + 13 = 48$, $5n = 35$ and $n = 7$.
Check: $\dfrac{12}{2} + \dfrac{6}{3} = 6 + 2 = 8$.

commonErrors.feedback: The equation was written as $\dfrac{n}{2} + 5 + \dfrac{n}{3} - 1 = 8$, which is a different instruction. 'Adds 5 and halves the result' puts the whole of $n + 5$ over the 2.

context.setting: Pure algebra, in the style of a mid-paper M3 item

scheme.examinerNote: (26x − 14)/24 from using 24 as the denominator earns M1 A1 and the final mark only if simplified.

hints: Find the lowest common multiple of 4 and 6.
Multiply each numerator by what its denominator was multiplied by.

commonErrors.feedback: Tops and bottoms were added separately. Over half the candidates in Summer 2025 M3 Q12 did not know where to start; the common denominator is always the first line.
The constants were not multiplied up: $3(3x + 1) = 9x + 3$ and $2(2x - 5) = 4x - 10$. The whole numerator is multiplied, not just the $x$ term.

context.setting: Pure algebra, a four-mark fractional equation in the style of a late M3 item

scheme.for: 8x + 6 − 5x + 10 = 40, both signs of the second bracket changed

hints: LCM of 5 and 2 is 10; the 4 on the right becomes 40.
parts.workedSolution:
Multiply every term by 10: $2(4x + 3) - 5(x - 2) = 40$.
Expand: $8x + 6 - 5x + 10 = 40$.
Collect: $3x + 16 = 40$, so $3x = 24$ and $x = 8$.
Check: $\dfrac{35}{5} - \dfrac{6}{2} = 7 - 3 = 4$.

commonErrors.feedback: $-5(x - 2)$ came out as $-5x - 10$, so the constant was $-4$ instead of $+16$. The minus multiplies both terms inside the bracket.
The 4 on the right was left unmultiplied, so the equation became $2(4x + 3) - 5(x - 2) = 4$. Every term on both sides takes the same multiplier, so the 4 becomes 40.

context.setting: Pure algebra, a single fraction then the equation it comes from

hints: 3 and 5 share no factor, so the LCD is 15.

commonErrors.feedback: The constants were not multiplied: $5 \times (-2) = -10$, not $-2$. The multiplier reaches every term of the numerator.

parts.stem: Hence solve $\dfrac{x - 2}{3} + \dfrac{x + 6}{5} = 6$. Give your answer as an exact value.

scheme.for: their single fraction set equal to 6 and the denominator cleared: 8x + 8 = 90

hints: Use your answer to part (a): one fraction equal to 6.
Multiply both sides by 15, so the 6 becomes 90.
$8x = 82$; leave the answer exact rather than rounding.

commonErrors.feedback: The answer was rounded when an exact value was asked for. $\dfrac{82}{8}$ is exactly 10.25, so nothing needs rounding here.

context.setting: A club membership split between two age groups

parts.stem:
A hockey club has $n$ members.

One third of the members are juniors. One fifth of the members, plus 8 more people, are coaches or helpers. Together the juniors and the coaches or helpers number 48.

Show that $\dfrac{n}{3} + \dfrac{n}{5} + 8 = 48$ and hence that $8n + 120 = 720$.

scheme.for: n/3 + n/5 + 8 = 48 written from the information
every term multiplied by 15 to reach 5n + 3n + 120 = 720, then 8n + 120 = 720 shown
scheme.examinerNote: The printed line must be reached by a forward chain; substituting a value earns nothing.

hints: Multiply every term by 15, the LCM of 3 and 5.
parts.workedSolution:
Juniors: $\dfrac{n}{3}$. Coaches or helpers: $\dfrac{n}{5} + 8$. Together: $\dfrac{n}{3} + \dfrac{n}{5} + 8 = 48$.
Multiply every term by 15: $5n + 3n + 120 = 720$, and $5n + 3n = 8n$, so $8n + 120 = 720$, as required.

commonErrors.feedback: The 8 was not multiplied by 15. Every term on both sides takes the same multiplier, so the 8 becomes 120.

parts.stem: Solve your equation to find the number of members in the club.
hints: The answer is a number of people, so it should be a whole number.
parts.workedSolution:
$8n + 120 = 720$ gives $8n = 600$, so $n = 75$ members.
Check: juniors $= \dfrac{75}{3} = 25$; coaches or helpers $= \dfrac{75}{5} + 8 = 15 + 8 = 23$; and $25 + 23 = 48$.

commonErrors.feedback: The 8 was treated as though it had already been multiplied, giving $8n = 480$. Keep the two stages separate: clear the fractions, then solve.

findTheMistake.stem: Sinéad was asked to solve $\dfrac{x}{4} + 3 = 9$. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The 3 on the left was not multiplied. Multiplying every term by 4 turns $\dfrac{x}{4}$ into $x$, the 3 into 12 and the 9 into 36.
findTheMistake.feedback: Choosing to multiply by 4 is the right method and earns the method mark. The 9 on the right was multiplied correctly, which shows the idea was understood; the 3 in the middle was simply missed. November 2024 M3 Q23 reported the same pattern: one term on a side multiplied and its neighbour left alone. A habit that fixes it: write the multiplier above every term before you start, then work along the line.

findTheMistake.stem: Ciarán was asked to write $\dfrac{4x - 1}{3} - \dfrac{x + 2}{4}$ as a single fraction. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: $-3(x + 2)$ is $-3x - 6$, not $-3x + 6$. The minus sign multiplies both terms of the bracket, so the $+2$ becomes $-6$.
findTheMistake.feedback: The common denominator and both bracketed numerators are right, so the first two marks stand. Line 3 is where it stops: the minus in front of the 3 travels into the bracket and reaches both terms. Writing $-3(x+2)$ as $-(3x + 6)$ first makes the second sign change impossible to miss. Summer 2025 M4 Q21 reported that only a small number reached full marks once more than one term had to be subtracted.

findTheMistake.stem: Niall was asked to solve $\dfrac{x}{2} + \dfrac{x}{3} = 10$. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: $\dfrac{1}{3}$ is not 0.33; it is $0.333\ldots$ . Rounding it at the very first line puts an error into everything that follows, and the exact answer is 12, not 12.048.
findTheMistake.feedback: The structure is sound and the arithmetic is carried out correctly, so the method mark is safe, and 12.0 is close enough to look right. The accuracy marks go because the very first line was already inexact. Summer 2023 M3 Q19 put it plainly: those who multiplied through by the common denominator succeeded; those who converted to decimals lost one or two marks to rounding. Clearing the denominators is also quicker.

prompts.prompt: The four moves for writing $\dfrac{ax+b}{p} \pm \dfrac{cx+d}{q}$ as a single fraction.
prompts.answer: 1 Lowest common denominator of $p$ and $q$. 2 Multiply each numerator by what its denominator was multiplied by, keeping it in a bracket. 3 Expand, changing every sign inside a subtracted bracket. 4 Collect like terms and check whether the fraction cancels.

prompts.prompt: Why must a subtracted numerator stay in a bracket?
prompts.answer: Because the minus sign belongs to the whole numerator. Removing the bracket changes the sign of every term inside it, and forgetting the second term is the most reported loss on this topic.

prompts.prompt: How do you start solving an equation with numerical denominators?
prompts.answer: Multiply **every** term on both sides by the lowest common denominator, and write that line down. The fractions disappear and an ordinary linear equation is left.

prompts.prompt: $\dfrac{x}{5} + 2 = 7$. What do the 2 and the 7 become when you multiply by 5?
prompts.answer: 10 and 35. Every term, on both sides, takes the multiplier — not only the fraction.

prompts.prompt: Why not turn the fractions into decimals?
prompts.answer: Because one third is $0.333\ldots$, so decimals force a rounding at the first line and the accuracy marks go with it. Keeping the fractions exact is both safer and quicker.

prompts.prompt: $\dfrac{2x + 1}{3} = 5$. What is the correct first line?
prompts.answer: $2x + 1 = 15$. Multiplying both sides by 3 cancels the denominator; multiplying the numerator by 3 as well would be doing it twice.
$\dfrac{aq + bp}{pq}$ — and if $p$ and $q$ share a factor, the lowest common denominator is smaller than $pq$ and keeps the numbers down.

prompts.prompt: How do you check a solution to a fractional equation?
prompts.answer: Substitute it back into the original equation and evaluate both sides. It takes ten seconds and catches sign slips that re-reading will not.

prompts.prompt: 'A number is increased by 5 and the result halved.' Write that in symbols.
prompts.answer: $\dfrac{n + 5}{2}$, with the whole of $n + 5$ over the 2. $\dfrac{n}{2} + 5$ is a different instruction.

prompts.prompt: Which fractional equations are NOT part of this topic?
prompts.answer: Any with the unknown in a denominator, such as $\dfrac{2}{x+1}$: those are M4, and they clear to a quadratic. Here the denominators are always numbers and the equation stays linear.

findings.asked: Solve an equation with fractions with numerical denominators.
findings.wentWrong: About a tenth got full marks. Those who multiplied through by 12 or used a common denominator of 12 succeeded; those who converted to decimals lost one or two marks through rounding.
findings.rule: Multiply every term by the LCM of the denominators; never switch to decimals.

findings.asked: Solve an equation with fractions and brackets.
findings.wentWrong: Generally well done. Decimal users again lost accuracy marks.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Either multiplied everything to remove the fractions, or found a common denominator and equated the numerators.
findings.rule: Two safe routes: clear all denominators, or common denominator then equate numerators.

findings.asked: Solve a fractional equation (part (c) of a harder algebra question).
findings.wentWrong: Only the best coped. A common error was multiplying the 4 by 3 but not the -2x term on the same side; many blanks suggested cross-multiplication was unfamiliar.
findings.rule: Whatever you multiply one term by, every term on both sides gets the same.

findings.wentWrong: Weaker candidates could not deal with the 3 in the denominator at all (zero). Others slipped on the final division or dropped a minus sign after a correct start (follow-through applied).
findings.rule: Remove the denominator first, then solve as a normal linear equation.

findings.asked: Add two algebraic fractions with numerical denominators.
findings.wentWrong: A third found the common denominator and added; over half did not know where to begin.
findings.rule: Common denominator, then combine the numerators.

findings.asked: Solve a linear equation with one fraction.
findings.wentWrong: Mostly right. Some multiplied the top of the fraction by 3 and the other side as well, which makes the first line wrong with nothing left to follow through; a common slip was subtracting 2 where it should have been added.
findings.rule: Multiplying by the denominator cancels it - do not also multiply the numerator.

findings.asked: A fractional equation with a bracket.
findings.wentWrong: Some could not deal with the 1/3 at all and scored zero; others expanded 3(3x - 1) wrongly but picked up follow-through.
findings.rule: Clear the fraction, then expand the bracket term by term.

insight.ruleToRemember: Multiply every term on both sides by the lowest common denominator and write that line down; keep fractions exact - converting to decimals costs accuracy marks.
insight.aStarSignal: Solving an equation with two different numerical denominators and a bracket in one clean sequence, with the common-denominator line visible.
